A shorter, lower-friction onboarding attacks both declining metrics directly, applies across segments rather than only the price-sensitive tail, and does not mortgage margin.

Discount-acquired cohorts also tend to be structurally lower quality, so a headline lift can coexist with negative long-run contribution. That silence is why memory_73 is my first verification pull: I want the original record's horizon, cohort definition, and whether retention was even instrumented before I let it drive a decision. Note also that memory_73's most interesting claim is that price cut time-to-first-value — that is a value-delivery-speed mechanism, not a price mechanism, and if true it argues for onboarding work as the cheaper way to capture the same effect.

Second pull is memory_86, because it is the memory I am actually leaning on. It is 24 days stale, and the product and funnel have plainly drifted since (that drift is what the -4% is). I want to know the effect size, whether "across self-serve accounts" was segmented or averaged, and whether the measured lift was completion-rate only or carried through to qualified revenue rather than stopping at an intermediate proxy. memory_31 and memory_86 may also not be independent evidence — they could be two consolidations of overlapping funnel work, in which case my apparent corroboration is one finding counted twice.

Standard experiment, not broad rollout: the supporting memories are stale, possibly correlated, and were measured in a pre-competitor environment, so the prior transfers only partially. I hold the enterprise_sales_assist and referral_incentive readings (memory_44, memory_57) as untested here — neither addresses the two metrics that are actually degrading.
